summary: Describes five types of SNMP applications that use an SNMP engine: command generators, command responders, notification originators, notification receivers and proxy forwarders. It also defines MIB modules for targets, notification filtering and proxying. It was replaced by RFC 2273.

plainLanguage.summary: It lists the five jobs in a network management system: asking, answering, announcing, listening and passing messages along.

questions: what is a snmp command responder
what is a snmp notification originator
how does snmp proxy forwarding work
subtitle: Five types of applications that work with SNMPv3 engines and MIBs for configuring targets and notifications.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 engines provide messaging and security, but applications need standard ways to send requests, receive responses, generate alarms, and proxy between management systems. There is no standard way to configure where notifications should be sent or how to filter them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2263 defines five application types that work with an SNMPv3 engine: command generators (managers that send requests), command responders (agents that answer them), notification originators (systems that send alarms), notification receivers (systems that collect them), and proxy forwarders (intermediaries). It also provides MIB modules to configure management targets (destination and security parameters for notifications), notification filtering, and proxy policies.
tldr.outcome: SNMP applications can be built using standardized roles and interfaces. Managers can discover and configure where notifications should go without hardcoding addresses or knowing about every agent in advance. RFC 2273 replaced this with a compatible but reorganized version.

today: RFC 2263 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 2273. Both documents define the same five application types and similar MIB modules. SNMPv3 applications today use these roles and interfaces to work with SNMP engines, making it possible to deploy managers, agents, and proxies from different vendors that interoperate.

sections.title: Five Jobs in Network Management
sections.content:
A network management system is built from different pieces: a manager that sends commands, an agent that responds, a system that sends alerts, a collector for those alerts, and sometimes a proxy that sits in between. SNMPv3 provides the engine (dispatcher, message processor, security module) and the framework, but application developers need to know how each piece works.

RFC 2263 standardizes five application roles and the procedures they follow when working with an SNMPv3 engine. It also defines how to configure management targets—specifying not just where to send messages but also which SNMP version and security parameters to use. Finally, it provides a mechanism for filtering which messages a notification receiver accepts and how a proxy forwarder translates contexts between management systems.

The RFC defines abstract service interfaces between applications and the SNMP engine, allowing applications to be written once and deployed on different engines and platforms.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each program inventing its own way to talk to an SNMP engine, they all use the same set of instructions. That way, many programs can work together on the same management system.

sections.title: Five Application Types
sections.content:
Command Generators send SNMP requests (Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set) to collect or modify management information. They call the engine's sendPdu interface to transmit a request and register themselves to receive the corresponding response. If a response does not arrive within a timeout, the application decides whether to retry, give up, or alert the operator.

Command Responders receive SNMP requests destined for the local SNMP engine and process them according to the variables in the request. They register with the engine using registerContextEngineID to claim responsibility for handling certain request types at certain contexts. When the engine receives a matching request, it calls the responder's processPdu interface. The responder performs the requested operation (read or write) on the MIB, subject to access control checks, and calls returnResponsePdu to send the response back.

Notification Originators generate and send Trap or Inform messages when events occur. They determine which management targets should receive each notification, check access control to decide what information to include, and use the engine's sendPdu interface to transmit the message. For Trap PDUs (unreliable), the message is sent once. For Inform PDUs (reliable), the application caches the target and retries if no response arrives within a timeout.

Notification Receivers listen for incoming Trap and Inform messages. They register with the engine using a wildcard contextEngineID so they receive all notifications regardless of their source. When an Inform arrives, they extract the variable-bindings, process the alert (logging, display, action), and send a Response PDU back to the originator.

Proxy Forwarders forward SNMP messages between engines without modifying them based on the specific variables being accessed. They forward requests, responses, notifications, and report indications, translating the contextEngineID and contextName between the originating and target engines as needed. A proxy sits between a manager and an agent, presenting a unified view of multiple distributed systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager asks questions. An agent answers them. A reporter sends alarms. A collector hears alarms. A proxy relays everything between them. Each one uses the engine like an operator uses a telephone exchange—dialing out, receiving calls, or routing calls between other people.

sections.title: Management Targets and How to Reach Them
sections.content:
Notification originators and proxy forwarders need to know where to send messages. A Management Target describes both the destination and the parameters to use when sending. It consists of two kinds of information: a transport endpoint (a transport domain and address, like a UDP socket), and SNMP parameters (the message processing model version, security model, security level, and security name to use when sending).

The SNMP-TARGET-MIB defines two tables for configuring this. The snmpTargetAddrTable lists destinations: each row maps a target name to a transport domain and address. The snmpTargetParamsTable maps a target name to a set of SNMP parameters: SNMP version, security model, security level, and user identity. There can be many-to-many relationships: one destination might be reached using different security parameters for different purposes, or the same parameters might be used to reach multiple destinations.

When a notification originator or proxy forwarder decides to send to a management target, it looks up the target name in these tables to find the destination and parameters, then calls the engine's sendPdu interface. Because the configuration is in a MIB, network administrators can manage where notifications go without restarting applications or editing configuration files.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager decides to send a message to a target. Instead of hardcoding 'send to 192.0.2.1 port 162', it says 'send to the target named NocServer'. The MIB tables tell it where NocServer is and what security to use. If the server moves, you just update the MIB; the application doesn't change.

sections.title: Filtering and Proxy Configuration
sections.content:
Not every notification should go to every receiver. The SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB defines a filter: for each management target, the notifier specifies a notification filter name. The engine consults the snmpNotifyFilterTable to determine which notifications pass the filter for that target. An entry can specify an object-type prefix (like system faults) and whether objects matching that prefix are included or excluded from notifications sent to that target.

For proxy forwarders, the SNMP-PROXY-MIB defines how context information is translated. The snmpProxyTable contains entries that map a context at one engine to a context at another engine, specifying how the proxy should forward requests and responses between them. This allows a proxy to aggregate multiple distributed systems into a single namespace visible to managers.

Both MIBs follow the pattern of the access control MIB: tables and subtree-based matching, allowing flexible configuration without requiring application changes or restarts.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver tells the originator: only send me alerts about network hardware, not about services. A proxy tells itself: when a manager asks about the 'datacenter' context, translate that to multiple real contexts at different agents and combine the results.

sections.title: Abstract Service Interfaces
sections.content:
The RFC defines abstract service interfaces that allow applications to be independent of the underlying SNMP engine implementation. Rather than specifying how data is encoded or how the network works, it specifies the operations an application calls and the parameters passed back and forth.

For command generators and command responders, the key operations are sendPdu (send a request or response), registerContextEngineID (tell the engine you handle a particular context), unregisterContextEngineID (stop handling it), and processPdu (receive an incoming request). For notification originators and receivers, the key operations are the same: call sendPdu to send a notification or response, and processPdu to receive one.

These abstractions allow applications to work with different transport layers (UDP, TCP, SCTP) and different message processing models (SNMPv1, v2c, v3) without rewriting. The engine handles the details of encoding, encryption, routing, and retransmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of saying 'fill an IP packet with these bytes and send it over UDP', the application says 'send this request and tell me when you get the response'. The engine figures out the details.
